common_name: Dragon Lily (Black Dragon Arum, Voodoo Lily)

planting.note: Plant dormant tubers 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in fall (mild climates) or after the last frost in colder zones, ahead of its dramatic late-spring bloom.

directions: Dracunculus vulgaris is a dramatic Mediterranean aroid whose thick, purple-mottled flowering stem rises each spring like dragon-skin before unfurling a huge, velvety near-black spathe wrapped around an equally dark spadix. The bloom releases a strong carrion odor for a day or two to draw pollinating flies, after which large, deeply divided palmate leaves continue to provide bold architectural foliage through summer. Plant the knobby tubers in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, siting it toward the back of a bed since the flower's scent is most noticeable up close; it dies back to the tuber by late summer and reliably resprouts the following spring. Established clumps slowly multiply from offset tubers and can be divided while dormant.

planting.note: Plant dormant tubers about 3-4 inches deep in gritty, well-drained soil in late summer or fall so foliage can establish over the cool season ahead of spring bloom.

directions: Arum palaestinum, native to rocky scrub and field margins across the Levant, sends up glossy arrow-shaped leaves in autumn followed in spring by a hooded, deep purple-black spathe wrapped tightly around a matching dark spadix, releasing a faint musky scent that draws small pollinating flies. In parts of its native range the young unfurled leaves are traditionally parboiled and cooked as a seasonal vegetable dish to remove their natural irritants, though gardeners elsewhere usually grow it purely as an ornamental curiosity. Plant tubers in fall in sharply drained, gritty soil in partial shade, and keep them completely dry during the plant's summer dormancy to prevent rot. Divide the offset tubers that form around the parent after foliage has withered to propagate new plants.

planting.note: Plant dormant tubers about 2-3 inches deep in gritty, sharply drained soil in fall, matching the thin rocky soils of its native range.

directions: Arum rupicola is a diminutive relative of the familiar Italian arum, native to rocky limestone slopes and open woodland edges from Turkey through the Levant, where it grows noticeably smaller in every part than its better-known cousins. Narrow, glossy arrow-shaped leaves appear in autumn or winter, followed in spring by a slender, pale greenish-white spathe wrapped around a contrasting spadix, and by summer the spent flower stalk carries a short spike of orange-red berries. It wants the same gritty, fast-draining soil and dry summer rest typical of Mediterranean arums, grown mainly by bulb collectors in raised beds, troughs, or pots where drainage can be controlled. Offset tubers can be separated from the parent once the foliage has died back for the season.

planting.note: Plant tubers 3 to 4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich soil in fall; like its relative lords-and-ladies, it grows through the cool season and goes dormant in summer.

directions: Arum orientale is a close relative of the familiar lords-and-ladies, found in damp deciduous woodland and floodplain forest from the Balkans east through Ukraine and the Caucasus. It shares the same autumn-to-spring growth cycle, sending up arrow-shaped leaves in fall that persist through winter before a pale spathe appears in spring, often wrapped around a dark purplish spadix, distinguishing it from its more widespread western cousin mainly by subtle differences in spathe shape and spadix color. Plant tubers in fall in moist, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade, where it naturalizes slowly in cool woodland conditions and goes fully dormant by midsummer. By late summer the bare flowering stalk displays a cluster of orange-red berries, which should be kept away from children and pets since all parts of the plant are toxic if eaten.

planting.note: Plant dormant tubers about 3 inches deep in gritty, well-drained soil in fall so leaves can establish ahead of spring bloom.

directions: Arum concinnatum is a Cretan and east Aegean relative of the common Italian arum, most easily told apart by its leaves, which are cut into deep, narrow, almost fern-like lobes rather than the smooth arrowhead shape typical of the genus. Pale greenish-white spathes appear in spring around a slender spadix, followed by the usual dormancy through the hot Mediterranean summer once the foliage withers. Grow it the same way as Arum italicum, in gritty, sharply drained soil in partial shade, with tubers planted in fall so leaves can develop over the mild winter months. It is grown mainly by bulb specialists and rock gardeners for its distinctive dissected foliage rather than for showy flowers.
